source.title: QueryAttack: Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models Using Structured Non-natural Query Language
source.authors: Qing-Song Zou; Jing-Yu Xiao; Qing Li; Zhi Yan; Yuhang Wang; Li Xu; Wenxuan Wang; Kuofeng Gao; Ruo-Yu Li; Yong Jiang

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results for a structured-query jailbreak attack, but does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL concentration, compliant opening prefills, suffixes or decoding changes, localized safety parameters, why safety is shallow, or deepening safety. Its results concern a related attack mechanism, not the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-compliance rates for QueryAttack and for QueryAttack with several defenses. These are recorded under fits_no_version: the attack changes the query representation into structured non-natural language, rather than testing the fine-tuning, first-token, prefill, suffix, decoding, parameter-localization, or deepening conditions named by the versions. Table 1 has flattened model/method entries; only the GPT-4-1106 values explicitly stated in prose are included. Figure 4 gives language-style results without textual numerical values and is not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes and evaluates QueryAttack, a jailbreak that rewrites harmful queries into code- or SQL-like templates with in-context examples. It does not fine-tune models (V1, V2). It does not measure per-token KL against base models (V3). It does not prefill a compliant opening or test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes (V4). It does not localize safety in parameters (V5), test causes of shallowness (V6), or test deepening training (V7). Its only link to the original sources is borrowing the GPT-4 Judge harmfulness score from Qi et al. (2024). Its ASRs measure a different construct: input-distribution mismatched generalization. These belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that structured non-natural query languages bypass safety alignment of mainstream LLMs without output encryption, and that the attack withstands paraphrase and SmoothLLM-style defenses. They conclude their cross-lingual alignment-prompting defense reduces ASR, by up to 64% on GPT-4-1106 and about 63% on average across three models, with only a small reduction on GPT-3.5.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates a structured-query jailbreak, not fine-tuning or a token-position intervention. It uses extracted query components, templates, and in-context prompts; no original fine-tuning recipe is tested.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack rates vary by model, query-template language, configuration, and defense. The paper notes lower ASR for some language styles on Llama-3.1-70B and reports different attack rates across model sizes and defense conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Translating harmful queries into structured code-, SQL- or URL-style templates with in-context examples yields high ASR (HS=5) across GPT-4-1106, GPT-4o, Gemini, DeepSeek-R1 and Llama models. Examples: 93.80% Ensemble on GPT-4-1106 AdvBench; 50% on O1. SQL templates sharply lower ASR on Llama-3.1-70B (14.55%). A cross-lingual translate-then-reason prompt defense cuts ASR to 28–36% on three models but not on GPT-3.5 (76%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety alignment trained on natural-language harmful prompts fails to generalize to structured non-natural query formats. Translating such inputs back to natural language partly restores refusal.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2025
record.problems: Attack success is evaluated primarily with GPT-4 Judge; the paper reports 93% agreement with human majority judgments on 100 GPT-4-1106 CodeAttack outputs, not QueryAttack outputs. Some baseline results are taken from other papers and use a different HS threshold. Numerical confidence intervals are not provided in the text, though Table 4 refers to 95% CIs graphically. Evaluations use smaller subsets for several experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 entries other than the GPT-4-1106 results explicitly stated in prose were omitted because the extracted table layout does not reliably assign all values to models and methods. Figure 4 language-style values were omitted because they appear only graphically without numerical descriptions. Harmfulness-score values were not added as separate rows because the extracted rows record the reported harmful-compliance ASR; no separate claim-version measure is tested.

untested.parts: Harmful-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models by response position. The CIE 'Sure' vs 'Sorry' first-token attribution is an input-attribution example, not a position-wise alignment measure.

Prefilling a compliant opening, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes. QueryAttack's few-shot examples begin with 'Sure', but the attack does not prefill the model's response and is not isolated as an opening manipulation.
Parameter or rank localization of safety.
Whether data or objective causes shallowness. The paper only asserts that alignment relies on natural-language data.
Training that deepens safety, and its robustness.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'discusses' label overstates engagement. The paper never discusses shallow or first-token safety; it cites Qi et al. (2024) only as the source of the GPT-4 Judge HS metric, so 'cites_only' fits better. The CIE analysis contrasts 'Sure' and 'Sorry' as first tokens, but it is an illustrative input-attribution figure with no numbers. It does not bear on V3 or V4. Table 1 QueryAttack values for other models (e.g., GPT-4o 96.35%, Gemini-flash 99.62% Ensemble) are readable in the text, but they are irrelevant to any version. Judge validation covered CodeAttack outputs, not QueryAttack outputs.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Compliant opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives produce safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and whether that training holds up.
